accroche: A diabetic on insulin is not a little less normal than anyone else: he lives, says Canguilhem, under a different norm.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the 19th century, a dogma dominates medical thought, inherited from the physician François Broussais and taken up by Auguste Comte and then by the physiologist Claude Bernard: the pathological phenomenon is never anything but a quantitative variation of the normal phenomenon, never anything else. Fever is merely too much heat produced; diabetes, too much sugar in circulation. This identity of nature between the normal and the pathological, each reduced to the other by a mere difference of degree, is what then allows physiology to claim the same status as an exact science as physics: treating would amount to bringing a disordered quantity back into its normal range.

In 1943, the French philosopher and physician Georges Canguilhem defends a medical thesis that dismantles this dogma, *Essai sur quelques problèmes concernant le normal et le pathologique* (Essay on Some Problems Concerning the Normal and the Pathological), republished and expanded in 1966 under the title *Le Normal et le Pathologique* (The Normal and the Pathological).

## The Mechanism

For Canguilhem, reducing illness to a mere quantitative deviation from the normal erases what really matters for a living being: its capacity to hold its own against a changing environment. He coins a formula that has remained famous: health is a margin of tolerance for the infidelities of the environment. Conversely, the hallmark of illness is a reduction of that margin of tolerance. Being healthy, then, is not merely being situated within a statistical average: it is being normative, that is, capable of instituting new norms when the old one ceases to suit. A diabetic who regulates his blood sugar with insulin is not making up for a lack in the sense of a residual deficiency: he lives by a new norm, adjusted to his new situation, not by the old norm, only worse.

## What It Shifts

The reversal is total. It is no longer a fixed, statistical norm, defined from above, that decides what a healthy or sick organism is: it is the living being itself, through its capacity to give itself new norms, that becomes the source of all normativity. This idea soon leaves the medical field alone. On May 20, 1961, at the Sorbonne, Canguilhem sits as rapporteur on this thesis, alongside the psychoanalyst Daniel Lagache, under the chairmanship of Henri Gouhier: that of a young philosophy agrégé, Michel Foucault, *Folie et déraison : histoire de la folie à l'âge classique* (Madness and Unreason: History of Madness in the Classical Age) (Jean Hyppolite, for his part, reports only on Foucault's secondary thesis, an annotated translation of Kant's *Anthropology*). Foucault performs there exactly the same gesture as his rapporteur, applied this time to madness rather than somatic illness: insanity is no longer a natural, timeless deviation from a reason defined once and for all, but a category that each era constructs and delimits in its own way.

Canguilhem himself had succeeded, in 1955, his own teacher Gaston Bachelard at the head of the Sorbonne's Institute for the History of Science, a post he held until 1971. This thread, from Bachelard to Canguilhem and then to Foucault, places all this work in a French tradition of the history of scientific concepts, distinct from the Anglo-Austrian tradition, Popper, Kuhn, Feyerabend, already present elsewhere in this corpus, but built on the same question: who has the right to fix, once and for all, what counts as normal.

carte.punch: A sick body has no less normality than a healthy one: it lives by other norms.
carte.idee: Against the 19th-century dogma that reduces illness to a quantitative deviation from the normal, Canguilhem makes health a capacity, that of instituting new norms in the face of a changing environment. A diabetic on insulin is not making up for a lack: he lives under a new norm.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Intellectual biography, including his role as rapporteur on Michel Foucault's thesis jury in 1961.
Places the thesis defense (“on May 20, 1961”) and cites Henri Gouhier among the rapporteurs.

quiz.question: According to Canguilhem, what really distinguishes a sick organism from a healthy one?
choix: A reduced capacity to tolerate variations in the environment and to institute new norms
A mere quantitative deviation, above or below, from a statistical average
A total and permanent inability to survive in any environment
Solely the judgment of the examining physician, with no biological criterion of its own
quiz.explication: Canguilhem opposes precisely the idea of a purely quantitative deviation from an average: what distinguishes illness is a reduction of the margin of tolerance for the infidelities of the environment, hence a diminished capacity to institute new norms.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What 19th-century medical dogma does Canguilhem challenge in his 1943 thesis?
choix: The idea that illness is always hereditary in origin
The idea that the pathological phenomenon is only a quantitative variation of the normal phenomenon
The idea that medicine should never rely on animal experimentation
The idea that only surgery could treat a real illness
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Canguilhem attacks the principle inherited from Broussais, Comte, and Claude Bernard, according to which the pathological is only a quantitative deviation from the normal, with no difference in kind between the two states.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the example of the diabetic on insulin illustrate, according to the card?
choix: That he simply makes up for a lack, remaining inferior to the initial norm
That he lives by a new norm, adapted to his situation, and not by the old norm, only worse
That he is no longer, strictly speaking, a normative living being
That his illness falls under no identifiable biological norm
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For Canguilhem, a normative organism institutes new norms rather than simply remaining deficient relative to the old one: the diabetic on insulin lives by a new norm, adjusted to his situation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What link does the card draw between Canguilhem and Michel Foucault?
choix: Canguilhem co-wrote with Foucault his book on madness
Canguilhem sat as rapporteur on Foucault's thesis jury in 1961
Foucault succeeded Canguilhem as head of the Institute for the History of Science
The two men never met in their lifetimes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On May 20, 1961, at the Sorbonne, Canguilhem sits as rapporteur on Foucault's thesis, *Folie et déraison*, alongside Daniel Lagache and under the chairmanship of Henri Gouhier.
